doc.title: 68088_Wilbur B. Ware, Sr oral history interview

chapter: Bass playing, avant-garde and the state of the music
title: Black and white points of view on jazz
summary: The pair discuss Benny Goodman as King of Swing, Max Roach's viewpoint, and critics preferring their own.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: King of Swing, they're serious about that. That is their point of view and they'll take somebody like Max Roach (PHONETIC) who say, "Well, hey, I don't see it that way at all." But his is another point of view. It's a black point of view.

Uh-huh. Well, it's going back to that black-white thing again. You notice most of the critics, they'll say, "Which is the better music? A black one or a white one?" You know, that's just like asking which came first, the chicken or the egg, you know.
Naturally white people are going to prefer white people.
And black people are going to prefer black people.
But you get somebody like -- what's the drummer's name? Was talking about he was looking for the source? Mel ?.
Yeah, that cat's been around for years.
If people are completely honest, then they recognize the true or the original source.
He went to Africa to find the source and he knows.
